---
title: "A loop your own class understands"
---

Your playlist keeps its songs in a chain of nodes, and every test in
`src/playlist.test.ts` is green. The page draws that chain by looping over
`playlist.toArray()`, which builds a fresh array just to throw it away after
the loop. Looping over the playlist itself feels like the obvious shortcut.
Type it and TypeScript stops you, with an error message worth reading slowly.

## The loop that refuses {#sec-iteration-experiment}

1. Open `coursework/playlist`, the app from the last chapter.

2. Create `src/scratch.test.ts` and ask for the loop you want:

   ```ts
   import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
   import { Playlist } from './playlist';

   describe('for...of', () => {
     it('walks the playlist', () => {
       const playlist = new Playlist();
       playlist.insertAtBeginning('Yellow', 'Coldplay');

       const titles: string[] = [];
       for (const song of playlist) {
         titles.push(song.title);
       }

       expect(titles).toEqual(['Yellow']);
     });
   });
   ```

3. Run `npm test`:

   ```text
    FAIL  src/scratch.test.ts > for...of > walks the playlist
   TypeError: playlist is not iterable
    ❯ src/scratch.test.ts:10:24
         8|
         9|     const titles: string[] = [];
        10|     for (const song of playlist) {
          |                        ^
        11|       titles.push(song.title);
        12|     }
   ```

4. Run `npx tsc --noEmit`, which says the same thing and names the missing
   piece:

   ```text
   src/scratch.test.ts(10,24): error TS2488: Type 'Playlist' must have a '[Symbol.iterator]()' method that returns an iterator.
   ```

`for...of` does not work on just anything: it asks the value on its right for a
method with the odd-looking name `[Symbol.iterator]()`, and that method is what
hands the loop one item after another. Arrays have it. So does the
`NodeList` that `querySelectorAll` gives back, which is why
`for (const paragraph of paragraphs)` has worked since Part 2. Your `Playlist`
is a class you wrote yourself, and nothing in it answers that question.

5. Change one thing in the loop and run `npm test` again:

   ```ts
   for (const song of playlist.toArray()) {
   ```

   Green. `toArray` walks the chain and builds an array, and `for...of` knows
   what to do with an array.

That is one way to visit every song, and for 20 songs it costs nothing you will
ever notice. It is still worth seeing the other way, because building a fresh
array on every redraw is work nobody asked for.

6. Delete `src/scratch.test.ts`. It has done its job.

## Handing the loop body to your class {#sec-iteration-foreach}

Instead of teaching `Playlist` the `[Symbol.iterator]()` trick, give it a method
that does the walking and takes the loop body as a parameter. Arrays offer that
method under the name `forEach`, and your class can offer it too:

```ts
forEach(callback: (song: Song) => void): void
```

Read the parameter type out loud as "a function that takes a `Song` and gives
nothing back". That is a **callback**, the same idea as in
@sec-callbacks-maps-callback: you hand another object a function, and that
object calls your function back when it has something for you. Every
`addEventListener` call you have written works this way.

Write the sentence first, in `src/playlist.test.ts`:

```ts
it('visits every song from front to back', () => {
  const playlist = new Playlist();
  playlist.insertAtBeginning('Yellow', 'Coldplay');
  playlist.insertAtBeginning('Roar', 'Katy Perry');
  playlist.insertAtBeginning('Believer', 'Imagine Dragons');

  const visited: string[] = [];
  playlist.forEach((song) => {
    visited.push(song.title);
  });

  expect(visited).toEqual(['Believer', 'Roar', 'Yellow']);
});
```

`npm test` goes red with `TypeError: playlist.forEach is not a function`, and
`npx tsc --noEmit` adds
`error TS2339: Property 'forEach' does not exist on type 'Playlist'.` Now make
it true, in `src/playlist.ts`:

```ts
forEach(callback: (song: Song) => void): void {
  let current = this.head;
  while (current !== null) {
    callback(current.value);
    current = current.next;
  }
}
```

That is the walk from `toArray` with one line swapped. Where `toArray` pushes
the song into an array, `forEach` hands it to the callback. The class keeps the
half that has to know about nodes and `next`, the caller keeps the half that
decides what happens to each song, and nothing outside `Playlist` ever touches
a `Node`.

Write one more sentence for this method: an empty playlist never calls the
callback. Count the calls in a `let` and expect 0.

## Counting without a counter {#sec-iteration-length}

The page wants a line that says how many songs are in the playlist, so
`Playlist` needs a `length`. Two more test sentences, and you write them the
same way, one at a time:

* a fresh playlist has a `length` of 0
* after two inserts and one delete, `length` is 1

A missing method and a missing getter fail differently, and both failures are
worth seeing once. `playlist.forEach(...)` on a class without `forEach` crashes
before the expectation is ever reached. `playlist.length` on a class without
`length` is simply `undefined`, so the test runs to the end and reports what it
compared:

```text
AssertionError: expected undefined to be +0 // Object.is equality

- Expected:
0

+ Received:
undefined
```

`npx tsc --noEmit` names the real cause either way:
`error TS2339: Property 'length' does not exist on type 'Playlist'.` Here is the
getter that makes both sentences true:

```ts
get length(): number {
  let count = 0;
  let current = this.head;
  while (current !== null) {
    count += 1;
    current = current.next;
  }
  return count;
}
```

A getter is read without parentheses, as you learned in
@sec-encapsulation-getters, so the page writes `playlist.length` and it looks
exactly like `songs.length` on an array. The two are not the same price. An
array stores its length as a plain number and hands that number over. Your
playlist counts from the head every single time somebody asks.

You could buy the cheap read: keep a private `count` field, start it at 0, and
change it in every method that adds or removes a song. Reading it is then one
step instead of one step per song. The bill arrives later, because
`insertAtBeginning`,
`insertAfter`, and `delete` each have to remember that extra line, and so does
every method you add to this class next month. Forget one of them and `length`
lies while the chain itself is still perfect. The wrong number shows up on the
page, far away from the method that caused it.

The walk pays on every read and can never go out of sync, because there is
nothing to keep in sync. A playlist holds a few dozen songs and redraws when the
user clicks, so pick the walk. When a structure grows long and something reads
its length many times a second, the counter starts to win, and the next chapter
has exactly that case.

## An array when you really need one {#sec-iteration-toarray}

`Playlist` now offers two ways to get at its songs, and they are for two
different jobs. Reach for `forEach` when you only visit, which covers drawing
one `<li>` per song and hunting for the longest title. Nothing new is built and
the songs stay in their nodes.

Reach for `toArray` when an array is what the next line actually needs. An index
is the clearest case, because `playlist.toArray()[0]` is the first song and
`forEach` has no way to express that. `reverse()` is another, and so is any code
that expects an array and will not take a callback. Your tests are that kind of
code: `expect(playlist.toArray()).toEqual([...])` needs a real array to compare
against.

::: {.callout-tip}
## For the curious

The `[Symbol.iterator]()` from the error message is real, and you can write it.
A class that has that method works with `for...of` like any array does. MDN
describes the rules under
[iteration protocols](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Iteration_protocols).
This course leaves the method out on purpose: writing one needs either a
generator function with `yield` or a hand-written object with a `next()` method,
and that is a lot of new syntax to buy a loop you can already write with
`forEach`.
:::

## Exercise: a playlist that counts itself {#sec-iteration-exercise}

Your `Playlist` class is tested and still knows nothing about the page. After
the first step, everything below happens in `index.html` and `src/index.ts`.

1. Run `npm test`. It reports four tests more than at the end of the last
   chapter: two for `forEach` and two for `length`.

2. Open `index.html` and add a paragraph for the count right above the element
   that shows the chain:

   ```html
   <p id="songCount"></p>
   ```

3. In `src/index.ts`, look that paragraph up next to the elements that are
   already there, and add it to the same null check.

4. Rewrite `renderChain()` so it asks `playlist.forEach(...)` instead of
   looping over `playlist.toArray()`. The body of your old loop becomes the
   body of the callback, mostly unchanged. Give `renderSongs()` the same
   treatment.

5. In `render()`, write the count into the new paragraph with a template
   string: `` `${playlist.length} songs` ``. A page that has just loaded says
   `0 songs`.

6. Also in `render()`, set `disabled` on the insert-after select to
   `playlist.length === 0`. An empty playlist has nothing to insert after, and a
   control that cannot do anything should look that way. The **Delete** buttons
   need no such line, because they leave the page together with their songs.

7. Run `npm start` and check all of it. Expected results:

   * a fresh page shows `0 songs` and a gray insert-after control
   * after adding two songs the line reads `2 songs`, the chain shows both, and
     the insert-after control works
   * after deleting both songs the line is back to `0 songs` and the control is
     gray again

8. Run `npm run verify`, which this project already has from the last chapter,
   fix what it reports, and commit.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

**One song, one word.** `1 songs` reads wrong. Make the line say `1 song` when
`playlist.length` is 1 and `songs` for every other number, 0 included.

**The chain backwards.** Add a button that draws the chain from the last song to
the first without changing the playlist itself. `forEach` cannot help, it only
ever walks forward. `playlist.toArray()` hands you an array that belongs to you,
`reverse()` flips that array, and the nodes stay exactly where they were.
:::
